name: Lena Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing is the hens, about six hundred layers in mobile houses that we tow round the fields every week. Then it's whatever the vegetables need, which in November is mostly leeks, kale and clearing beds for winter. The farm's organic and fairly small, it belongs to Gwen and Alan, who are in their late sixties and still out in the yard every day. Twice a week I pack the veg boxes for the farm shop, and on Fridays I write the little newsletter that goes in them, which I secretly love.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Wet ground wears me out, and moving electric fencing for the sheep in the dark at four in the afternoon. What keeps me there is that Gwen and Alan treat me like I'll run the place one day, which I might. My partner Sam's a nurse at the district hospital, so between us we're doing all right, and we've got a good bit saved, about ten months of my wages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll ask a chatbot to tidy up the newsletter if I'm tired, or check a rotation idea, but I double-check everything with Alan's notebooks. Gwen calls it my oracle and rolls her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problems, like soil and the price supermarkets pay for milk. I'd probably post something cheeky on the farm's page about our hens not being replaced by an app any time soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing much changes for me, and I'm fine with that. I'd keep using the chatbot for the newsletter, because it does save me half an hour on a Friday. My worries would be the same ones I have now, the weather and whether Gwen and Alan can keep the place going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, basically. I'd keep putting money aside with Sam, and keep learning the bits of the business Alan does, like the accounts and the organic inspections, because that's where my future is anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit disappointed, maybe, because I like a good shake-up when it's not my job being shaken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit disappointed. What were you hoping AI might do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Help with the weeding, honestly. Organic means hand-weeding the carrot beds, and there's a robot weeder I saw on a video that looked brilliant. If it all turns out to be hype, I'm still on my knees in the carrots in June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Gwen and Alan about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they can stop worrying I'll be replaced by a laptop. Alan reads every scary headline aloud at tea break, so it would be nice to give him one less thing.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about the real problems, like soil and what supermarkets pay farmers. I'd post something cheeky about our hens not being replaced by an app any time soon.
S0.think: Privately it means nothing much changes, and I'm fine with that. I'd still use the chatbot to save half an hour on the newsletter, and my real worries would stay the weather and the farm's future.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving with her partner as before. Keeps learning the accounts and organic inspection side of the business from the owner, Alan.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small disappointment that the robot weeder she hoped for wouldn't arrive.
S0.quote: If it all turns out to be hype, I'm still on my knees in the carrots in June.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is the rare person who'd be mildly disappointed by AI fizzling out, because she hoped it would take the worst manual job off her. She sees her future in taking over the farm, not in technology. Her tone was relaxed and warm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's always changed, my grandmother went from horses to tractors and nobody marched about that. But I'd also say the government has to make sure the seasonal pickers and the older workers don't get thrown off. People like Mihai, who comes every summer for the harvest, are the first ones nobody thinks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's probably more good than bad. A small organic farm will never be the first to get robots, and if the weeding gets automated, I'd be glad. What I'd worry about is the big conventional farms round us going fully automatic and making our prices look silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the neighbours did first, especially the Hendersons up the lane, because they buy every new gadget. If the robot weeder worked for them for a season, I'd ask Gwen and Alan to share one with two other organic farms nearby. And I'd do one of those short online courses on farm software, just so I'm not the one in the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. It's more about the farm than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait for the Hendersons to try things first. Is that how you usually work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much. Let someone else find out what breaks. The Hendersons bought a drone last year and crashed it into the hedge twice in a week, and I learned more from watching them than from any advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what about Mihai? What would you actually do for someone like him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure Gwen keeps hiring him for the jobs a machine still can't do well, like grading the squash. I'd also sign whatever petition there was for seasonal workers to get help retraining. It's not much, but it's what I'd actually do rather than just say.

S1.say: I'd say farming has always changed, from horses to tractors. But the government has to make sure seasonal pickers and older workers aren't thrown off.
S1.think: For me it's probably more good than bad, because a small organic farm won't be first to get robots and I'd love the weeding automated. I'd worry about big conventional farms nearby undercutting our prices.
S1.do: Watches how the neighbouring Hendersons manage new kit for a season, then proposes sharing a robot weeder with two other organic farms. Takes a short online course in farm software and signs petitions for seasonal worker retraining.
S1.feel: Uneasy but able to live with it, worried more for the farm than for herself.
S1.quote: The Hendersons bought a drone last year and crashed it into the hedge twice in a week, and I learned more from watching them than from any advert.
S1.fieldNote: She thinks about the farm as a shared project and about seasonal workers before herself. Her habit of letting neighbours test new kit first is a deliberate strategy, not reluctance. She separated what she'd say from what she'd actually do, and kept the promises small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what happens when nobody regulates tech companies, and I'd be furious about it in public. I'd push for some kind of basic income or wage support, loudly. And I'd point out that if robots can do nursing too, it's not just us farmers, it's everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it hits both of us at once, me and Sam. Hospitals would get the robots and the AI before small farms do, so Sam might go first, which turns everything upside down. Our savings would carry us for a bit, but I don't know what either of us would be for after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Sam and I would stop paying into the house deposit and keep it as cash, because I'd want it easy to reach. I'd join the farmworkers' union, which I keep meaning to do, and I'd turn up to anything that pushed for income support. And I'd sit down with Gwen and Alan and ask straight out what they'd do if a company offered to buy the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just imagining that conversation with Gwen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why that conversation in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the farm is my plan. If they're tired and someone waves money at them, I don't blame them for taking it, but then my whole picture of the next twenty years is gone. That's worse than losing the job, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning do, compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give us time to do anything clever. I couldn't learn a whole new trade in that time, and Sam couldn't either. All we could really do is hold on to the money and lean on each other and whatever help the government finally puts together.

S2.say: I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates tech companies, and I'd push loudly for basic income or wage support. If robots can do nursing too, it isn't just farmers, it's everyone.
S2.think: It would hit both me and my partner at once, and the hospital might automate before our small farm does. Our savings would carry us a while, but I don't know what either of us would be for after that.
S2.do: Pauses paying into the house deposit and keeps it as easy-to-reach cash. Joins the farmworkers' union, backs campaigns for income support and asks the farm owners directly what they'd do if a company offered to buy them out.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach dropping at the thought of the farm being sold.
S2.quote: If they're tired and someone waves money at them, I don't blame them for taking it, but then my whole picture of the next twenty years is gone.
S2.fieldNote: Her deepest fear here is losing the farm she expects to take over, more than losing wages. She was the first to think about her partner's job being exposed too. With only two years, she falls back on money, each other and public help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as with the fast one, that we need a plan from the government, and five years is enough to make one. I'd say farms like ours should get help to stay in local hands rather than be bought up. People might roll their eyes, but I'd keep saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time for me to make a choice, which feels very different. I could try to buy into the farm with Gwen and Alan, or I could train for something else. Either way, I'm not just standing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask Gwen and Alan about a proper plan for me to buy a share, using some of our savings. I'd look at a part-time course in teaching or care farming, the kind where people come to the farm for therapy, because a robot can't really do that well. I'd keep using the AI tools a bit more, but only for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the kind where I'm busy, not frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care farming is quite a specific idea. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt runs a day centre, and they used to bring a group of their clients to our farm in summer to collect eggs. One lad, Robbie, who never spoke much, used to name every hen. That's work where being a person is the whole point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be buying into a farm in a world where robots could run it. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I've thought about it. Land is still land, and if the farm becomes a place people visit rather than a place that just grows food, it still needs someone who cares. I'd rather gamble on that than on a job I don't know yet.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the government to make a plan, and farms like ours should get help to stay in local hands. People might roll their eyes, but I'd keep saying it.
S3.think: Five years is enough time to make a real choice, which feels completely different from two. I could buy into the farm or train for something else, but either way I'm not just standing there.
S3.do: Asks the owners in the first year for a plan to buy a share of the farm using some savings. Looks into a part-time course in care farming or teaching and uses AI tools more, but only for paperwork.
S3.feel: Anxious, but busy rather than frozen.
S3.quote: One lad, Robbie, who never spoke much, used to name every hen. That's work where being a person is the whole point.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years changed her from holding on to choosing. Her care-farming idea grew from a specific memory, which made it feel like a real plan. She knowingly accepted the risk of buying land in a robot world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it like we wasted the warnings about climate. I'd want proper public retraining, and a say for workers in how the robots get used. That's the kind of thing I'd write to the local paper about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'm less worried about me than about the bigger choices, like whether Sam and I have children into that world. I'd be thirty-seven. That's the question that would keep coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the share in the farm, but slowly, maybe over three or four years. I'd wait a year or two to see which robots actually work on small farms before training on anything. And Sam and I would have the children conversation properly, which we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly thoughtful. It's more a big question than a fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to know before having that conversation with Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether there's going to be work for people at all, or some kind of income that doesn't depend on it. And whether our area stays a place with people in it, not just machines in fields. I'd want to know there'd be other kids at the village school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said with ten years you'd still wait a year or two. Why wait if you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first robots are always the ones that crash into the hedge. I'd rather spend my time and our savings on the ones that have proven themselves. Ten years means I can afford to be second, not first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it like we wasted warnings about climate. I'd want public retraining and a say for workers in how the robots are used.
S4.think: With ten years I worry less about my job and more about whether my partner and I should have children into that world. I'd be thirty-seven, and that question would keep coming back.
S4.do: Buys a share in the farm slowly over three or four years. Waits a year or two to see which robots work on small farms before training, and finally has the conversation about children with her partner.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly thoughtful, more a big question than a fear.
S4.quote: I'd want to know there'd be other kids at the village school.
S4.fieldNote: Time turned her worry from work towards family, and the question of children came up on its own. She used the extra decade to be second rather than first, which matches how she treats new kit already. Her public line stays political, while her private one is about her household.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits Sam and me together with no time to think. What would help is some kind of guaranteed income while people retrain, and help for farms like Gwen and Alan's to stay with the people who work them rather than be sold to whoever has the most money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but someone has to decide what a robot does when a ewe's struggling to lamb at two in the morning. I'd want that to still be a person who cares, whatever else changes.

headlineQuote: Someone has to decide what a robot does when a ewe's struggling to lamb at two in the morning.
portrait: Lena Quinn, 27, works on a small organic farm with hens, sheep and vegetables, owned by an older couple who treat her as their likely successor. She lives with her partner Sam, a nurse, and uses AI tools now and then for the farm shop newsletter. She'd be a little disappointed by the AI Plateau, waits for neighbours to test new kit under Steady Disruption, and is alarmed by AGI by 2028 because it would hit her and Sam together and could cost her the farm. With more warning she plans to buy into the farm and look at care farming, and her worries shift to whether to have children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would hit her and her partner's jobs at the same time with no time to think.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income while people retrain, and help for small farms to stay with the people who work them instead of being sold off.
